questions.prompt: How should production differ from staging in a well built setup?
options: Same code with different variable values
questions.explanation: Reusing the code is what makes a staging test meaningful for production.

questions.prompt: What does prevent_destroy protect against?
options: Accidental removal of a resource that must not be deleted
questions.explanation: It is the guardrail for things like a production database.

questions.prompt: Why list every internet reachable resource and justify each one?
options: Because anything reachable is attack surface that must be intentional
questions.explanation: Exposure that nobody decided on is the most common way systems get compromised.

questions.prompt: What should you do with an IAM permission you cannot justify?
options: Remove it and confirm nothing broke
questions.explanation: Unjustified permissions accumulate until a small compromise becomes a large one.

questions.prompt: Where can secrets end up even when they are not in your code?
questions.explanation: State stores real attribute values, which is why the backend must be protected.

questions.prompt: Why compare your real cost against your original estimate?
options: Because the gap teaches you where your architectural intuition is wrong
questions.explanation: Estimating badly is normal, and only the comparison improves it.

questions.prompt: How should you right size a resource?
questions.explanation: Right sizing without data is just a different guess.

questions.prompt: Why must the architecture diagram match the code exactly?
options: Because people make decisions from the diagram and a stale one misleads them
questions.explanation: An inaccurate diagram is worse than none, because it is trusted.

questions.prompt: What should a runbook cover?
options: Deploy, rollback, restore and the most likely failures
questions.explanation: It exists to be followed under pressure by someone who is not you.

questions.prompt: Why clone your own repository to a clean machine before calling it finished?
options: Because your instructions almost certainly assume something only your machine has
questions.explanation: It is the same works on my machine problem applied to documentation.

questions.prompt: What number makes the strongest impression in a project write up?
options: Time to recovery after a deliberate failure
questions.explanation: Recovery time shows you can operate a system, not just build one.

questions.prompt: Why record the monthly cost in the README?
options: Because knowing what your architecture costs is part of the job
questions.explanation: Engineers who cannot answer what it costs get caught out in interviews and at work.

questions.prompt: A design decision is more valuable in a write up when you also state what you rejected.
questions.explanation: The rejected alternative is what shows you considered trade offs rather than followed a tutorial.

questions.prompt: If a clean clone cannot follow your instructions, the project is not actually finished.
questions.explanation: Reproducibility by someone else is the standard, not reproducibility by you.

questions.prompt: Encryption at rest and encryption in transit are the same protection.
questions.explanation: One protects stored data and the other protects data moving across a network, and you need both.

questions.prompt: What does Kubernetes provide that a single container host does not?
options: Scheduling, self healing and declarative desired state across many machines
questions.explanation: It manages containers across a fleet rather than on one box.

questions.prompt: What is the desired state loop?
options: The controller continuously reconciling actual state toward what you declared
questions.explanation: You declare what you want and the system keeps working to make reality match.

questions.prompt: What happens when you delete a pod managed by a deployment?
questions.explanation: The deployment holds the replica count, so it restores it.

questions.prompt: What is a service in Kubernetes?
options: A stable way to reach a changing set of pods
questions.explanation: Pods come and go, so the service provides a consistent address.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a ConfigMap?
options: Passing non sensitive configuration into pods
questions.explanation: It keeps configuration out of the image, the same principle you learned on day 88.

questions.prompt: Where would you look first for a pod stuck in a crash loop?
options: The pod logs and describe output
questions.explanation: Describe shows events and logs show why the process exited.

questions.prompt: A pod is stuck in pending. What is the usual cause?
options: It cannot be scheduled, often for lack of resources
questions.explanation: Pending means the scheduler has not placed it, and the events explain why.

questions.prompt: When would ECS be a better choice than Kubernetes for a small team?
options: When you want containers running without the operational overhead of a cluster
questions.explanation: Kubernetes brings real capability and real complexity, and small teams often need only the first part.

questions.prompt: Why delete a managed cluster the same day you create it?
options: Because the control plane and nodes bill continuously
questions.explanation: A forgotten cluster is one of the more expensive things to leave running.

questions.prompt: How should you describe your Kubernetes level in an interview after one week?
options: Honestly, as exposure with a plan to go deeper
questions.explanation: Overclaiming collapses on the first follow up question, and honesty with a plan reads well.

questions.prompt: What operational cost does Kubernetes add?
options: Cluster upgrades, networking complexity and more moving parts to monitor
questions.explanation: The platform itself becomes something you have to run and maintain.

questions.prompt: Which earlier skill transfers directly to debugging inside a pod?
options: Your Linux and networking troubleshooting from Months 1 and 2
questions.explanation: A container is a normal Linux environment, so the same tools and method apply.

questions.prompt: One week is enough to become competent at Kubernetes.
questions.explanation: One week gives you working familiarity, and real competence takes months of use.

questions.prompt: The declarative model in Kubernetes is conceptually similar to how Terraform works.
questions.explanation: Both take a desired state and work to make reality match it.

questions.prompt: Writing an honest Phase 2 plan is more useful than pretending the week made you job ready on Kubernetes.
questions.explanation: A clear plan shows self awareness, which interviewers read as maturity.

questions.prompt: What should you do before sending the first application?
options: Update the CV and portfolio with your capstone and its outcomes
questions.explanation: The materials are what every application depends on, so they come first.

questions.prompt: Why keep an application tracker?
options: Because follow ups and patterns are impossible to manage from memory
questions.explanation: Without a record you will forget who to chase and what worked.

questions.prompt: Why tailor each application rather than sending the same CV everywhere?
options: Because a targeted application is read and a generic one is filtered
questions.explanation: Volume without relevance produces silence, which people then mistake for a skills problem.

questions.prompt: What is the value of messaging a person rather than only applying online?
options: Applications attached to a real conversation get read far more often
questions.explanation: A human contact moves you out of an anonymous pile.

questions.prompt: What should you do when the same requirement appears in many postings and you lack it?
options: Note it and plan how to close that gap next
questions.explanation: The postings are free market research about what to learn next.

questions.prompt: Why present your capstone in ten minutes with a diagram?
options: Because you will be asked to explain a project and rambling loses the room
questions.explanation: A rehearsed, structured walkthrough is one of the highest value things you can practise.

questions.prompt: Why decide your response to rejection before it happens?
options: Because deciding in advance stops one rejection from ending the search
questions.explanation: The plan protects you at the moment your judgement is worst.

questions.prompt: What makes a good outreach message?
options: A long summary of your CV
Something short and specific about their work
questions.explanation: Specific and brief gets replies, while generic and long does not.

questions.prompt: Why research salary ranges before interviews?
options: So you are not caught unprepared by the question
questions.explanation: Being asked with no answer prepared puts you in a weak position immediately.

questions.prompt: Which roles should be in your first batch of applications?
options: Trainee, cloud support and junior cloud titles
questions.explanation: These are the doors that genuinely open at this stage, as established earlier.

questions.prompt: Why set a weekly application rhythm rather than applying in bursts?
options: Because the search continues past the end of the plan and needs a sustainable pace
questions.explanation: A burst then silence is the pattern that produces nothing.

questions.prompt: What questions are worth asking an interviewer?
options: How they deploy, how they handle incidents, and how on call works
questions.explanation: Those questions show you understand that systems have to be run, not just built.

questions.prompt: Preparing references properly before you need them is part of an organised search.
questions.explanation: Being asked for references and having none ready costs you time at the worst moment.

questions.prompt: Sending thirty tailored applications is likely to outperform sending three hundred generic ones.
questions.explanation: Relevance beats volume, and generic applications rarely get past the first filter.

questions.prompt: Following up politely on an old application is unprofessional.
questions.explanation: A brief, polite follow up is normal and sometimes the reason an application gets seen at all.

questions.prompt: What is the point of doing a retention audit with no notes?
options: To find out what you actually retained rather than what you completed
questions.explanation: Completion and retention are different things, and only one of them shows up in an interview.

questions.prompt: What should you do with the list of things you have forgotten?
options: Drill the most important items until you can do them unaided
questions.explanation: The list is the whole value of the exercise, and acting on it is the point.

questions.prompt: Why rebuild an environment from an empty directory?
options: Because it measures what you can do without lookups
questions.explanation: Counting the lookups gives you an honest measure of real fluency.

questions.prompt: Why write an honest paragraph about your current level?
options: Because both overclaiming and underclaiming cost you in interviews
questions.explanation: Accurate self assessment is what lets you target the right roles and answer questions credibly.

questions.prompt: Why choose your next project before finishing this one?
options: So there is no empty week where the habit dies
questions.explanation: The gap after a big finish is where momentum is usually lost.

questions.prompt: What is a sustainable pace after an intensive plan ends?
options: The same six hours a day
Smaller than before, but never zero
questions.explanation: Skills decay, and a small daily floor preserves far more than sporadic bursts.

questions.prompt: Why set a monthly date to re-audit retention?
options: Because unused skills fade and you need to know which ones are fading
questions.explanation: A scheduled check catches decay before an interview does.

questions.prompt: What makes a beginner's honest account worth publishing?
options: Because a truthful record of struggle is more useful than another polished tutorial
questions.explanation: People starting where you started need it, and it demonstrates communication as well.

questions.prompt: What is a realistic expectation after finishing this plan?
options: Trainee or support level opportunities, with a real role likely further out
questions.explanation: This matches the honest assessment made at the start, and expecting it prevents quitting.

questions.prompt: Why did the deliberate breakage exercises matter most?
options: Because diagnosing real faults is the skill employers actually test
questions.explanation: Anyone can follow a tutorial, and very few candidates can debug something they did not expect.

questions.prompt: What should be reachable from your GitHub profile at the end?
options: Your best projects with diagrams, READMEs and clean history
questions.explanation: A reviewer spends minutes, so the best work must be immediately visible.

questions.prompt: What does finishing the plan actually mean?
options: One stage is complete and the next one starts tomorrow
You are job ready for any role
questions.explanation: The plan ending and the work ending are not the same thing.

questions.prompt: Being able to complete a task with notes is the same as being able to do it in an interview.
questions.explanation: Interviews and incidents happen without your notes, which is why unaided drilling matters.

questions.prompt: Deciding exactly what you will do the day after the plan ends protects the habit you built.
questions.explanation: The undefined day after a finish line is where most people stop.

questions.prompt: An honest account of what you still cannot do makes your claims about what you can do more credible.
questions.explanation: Calibrated self assessment is read as maturity, and it is rare enough to stand out.
